threats.defense: A procedural Chain-of-Verification firewall verifies every claim in pure Python — stop-word filtering, Jaccard similarity, constraint-denial detection — with no model inside it. When no claim survives as Entailment, a minimum-survivor rule overrides the verdict to "insufficient verifiable evidence" and the case goes to a human.
threats.threat: The Judge asserts a conclusion no evidence supports — a confident sentence with nothing under it.

threats.defense: One append-only event stream with a single registered backend per process, a closed scalar payload catalog, and reads only through the registered reader — never by parsing the raw file.
threats.threat: Two processes each write their own copy of the audit stream, so the record of what happened depends on which host you ask.

threats.defense: Workflow states are validated models, not bare enums: each carries a stable identifier, a definition, and its set of allowable next states, so an illegal transition is unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged. Only a human can set the terminal rejection.
threats.threat: Code moves a case into a state it should not be able to reach — for example marking a case rejected without a human.

threats.defense: The run suspends on a LangGraph interrupt. Nothing outbound leaves and no durable artefact is written until a named reviewer resumes it, and the resume itself is an audited event.
threats.threat: The agent quietly does something durable — sends a message, writes to a system of record — without anyone confirming it.
